projects.title: VEX Robotics

blocks.text: I was the team captain, design, and programming lead for team 7614A, representing Newmarket High School. I was responsible for end-to-end development and design of the robot. We competed in four seasons of the VEX V5 Robotics Competition, achieving accalades on the regional and provincial scale.

blocks.text: Our team implemented a seven step engineering design process. We applied this process to multiple design cycles per season, resulting in robots iterations that quantifiably improved as the season progressed. I led the documentation of our design cycles in engineering notebooks, which led us to winning numerous judged awards.

items.caption: 2025 Provincials Robot and the season's trophies
2026 Provincials Robot and the season's trophies

blocks.text: I led the usage of Fusion 360 to design entire robots and prototypes before assembly, ensuring that all geometries and assemblies would work well together. I led the use of CNC milling on custom plastic pieces designed in CAD. We used DFM and DFA as foundational design philosophies in order to streamline the building process.

Using PID loops and field-wide global odometry , I was able to achieve consistent and efficient autonomous movement from robots. A custom, in-house library increased efficiency while programming and tuning, allowing for more time spent on refining the mechanical aspects of the robot. Furthermore, the sophisticated use of various sensors allowed for more accurate and responsive control systems, allowing for adaptive autonomous behavior. All of the routes shown below are fully autonomous, with zero human intervention.

projects.title: 3 DOF Humanoid Arm

blocks.text:
I created a 3 degree-of-freedom lower humanoid arm, that I designed, simulated, and optimized in Solidworks. The first iteration consisted of three joints: the forearm, wrist, and gripper. Each added a degree of freedom, allowing for forearm rotation, wrist flexion, and object grasping, replicating the core motions of a human lower arm.

The gripper uses a double slider crank to convert the actuator’s motion into linear motion for the jaws, as shown in the GIF above.

The second iteration of the arm focused on redesigning the gripper and wrist to improve manufacturability, assembly, and structural rigidity. The linkages in the gripper were replaced with ball bearings and shoulder bolts, allowing for less slop and lower friction in each linkage.

The gripper was redesigned to be more compact, while the wrist was redesigned to allow for easier assembly and manufacturing. Furthermore, I redesigned the fingers to be printed of TPU, which allows for high flexibility and confirmation to the shapes that it interacts with.

projects.title: bezier buddy

blocks.text:
My team and I at YR Hacks 2025 created a 4-motor holonomic drivetrain from scratch. We added parallel and perpendicular tracking wheels to implement odometry.

The goal was to create a tool to help students understand Bézier curves and the control algorithms that enable robots to follow them. We created a web application that could take in various points on a Cartesian plane and output a Bezier curve that could be fed into the pure pursuit library for the drivetrain.

We created the drivetrain from a mix of 3d printed gussets and VEX V5 robotics parts. We also used CNC-milled polycarbonate pieces to create custom tracking wheel sleds, allowing for dynamic position tracking. The robot itself is a X-drive, using omni wheels in a X-shape pattern, to allow for side-to-side strafing, as well as front-and-back driving.

items.caption: The custom polycarbonate sleds for the dead tracking wheels.

blocks.text: Developed a custom C++ Pure Pursuit library for our holonomic drivetrain, allowing the robot to autonomously follow smooth Bézier curves with precision. The Pure Pursuit algorithm works by continuously looking ahead along a planned path, selecting a target point, and adjusting the robot’s movement to steer toward it as it progresses along the curve.

items.caption: A visual representation of the Pure Pursuit algorithm, showing the robot's current position, the lookahead point, and the path it is following.
A video of the robot following a Bézier curve using the Pure Pursuit algorithm.

blocks.text: To make path creation easier, we also built a JavaScript path planner that lets users click waypoints on the field, automatically generates smooth Bézier curves between them, and exports field-scaled coordinates ready to use in the robot’s autonomous code. Together, these tools made it easier to design, visualize, and execute smooth, efficient, and accurate autonomous movements.
